meta.description: Important limitations and context-sensitivity of human-patterned language rules. These caveats should be surfaced alongside any rules to prevent misapplication.
meta.usage: Call humanizer_get_caveats during any rewrite to check that the layer-level rules are not over-applied. The ethical_considerations block constrains the legitimate use cases for the whole tool.

core_caveats.statement: Human-likeness is a probabilistic judgment, not an authorship determination.
core_caveats.explanation: These rules describe statistical tendencies, not absolute markers. Text that follows every rule may still be flagged by some detectors. Text that breaks many rules may still read as human. The goal is to shift the probability distribution, not to guarantee a particular outcome.

core_caveats.statement: High perplexity does not imply creativity or quality.
core_caveats.explanation: Unusual word choices can signal human authorship or they can signal confused, unclear writing. The goal is contextually appropriate unpredictability (surprising choices that still fit), not randomness.

core_caveats.statement: High burstiness does not imply authenticity or originality.
core_caveats.explanation: Structural variation signals human writing patterns, but mechanical variation (randomly alternating long and short sentences) is itself detectable. The variation should feel motivated by the content, not imposed as a pattern.

core_caveats.statement: ESL writing may align with AI patterns without being AI-generated.
core_caveats.explanation: Writers whose first language is not English may produce text that follows instruction-driven structure, uses formulaic transitions taught in language courses, shows lower lexical diversity in English, and exhibits other patterns that overlap with AI-generated text. Aggressive application of HPL rules to ESL text risks erasing the writer's voice or overcorrecting natural L2 patterns. Apply rules with awareness that what looks like an AI pattern may be a learner pattern.

core_caveats.statement: Professionally edited prose may reduce human markers.
core_caveats.explanation: Professional editing naturally smooths out some cognitive load artifacts, self-monitoring traces, and punctuation drift. A heavily edited human text may share some statistical properties with AI text. The goal of HPL is not to undo professional editing but to ensure that editing didn't remove all human texture.

core_caveats.statement: Detection features are context-sensitive, degrade under domain shift, and are affected by revision.
core_caveats.explanation: A rule that reliably distinguishes AI text in news articles may not work for academic papers or social media posts. Detectors trained on one LLM may not generalize to others, and rules tuned for blog posts can misfire on academic text. Apply rules through the content_profiles layer, which adjusts aggressiveness by content type, and treat cross-domain results with skepticism.
core_caveats.history: Ardeshirifar (2025) quantifies this risk: F1 scores dropped 34.67 percentage points when a hand-crafted feature classifier trained on one dataset (HC3) was tested on text from a different model generation (GPT-2).

core_caveats.statement: As language models evolve, detection patterns shift.
core_caveats.explanation: The specific flagged words and patterns in this system reflect tendencies observed in models through 2025 (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA, Falcon, Mistral). Newer models may adopt different patterns. The structural and psycholinguistic rules are more durable than the lexical ones, which may need periodic updating.

core_caveats.statement: Lexical over-regularization and common discourse scaffolding are frequently weighted as machine-correlated features despite their prevalence in academic and journalistic norms.
core_caveats.explanation: Some patterns flagged as AI-correlated (formulaic transitions, standardized grammar, neutral tone) are conventional in certain human writing contexts. The rules account for this through content_profiles, but users should exercise judgment when the detected pattern is actually genre-appropriate.

core_caveats.statement: Applying human-patterning rules uniformly is itself an AI signal.
core_caveats.explanation: This is the most important caveat. If every paragraph ends on the same kind of closer, turns on the same contrast or opens with the same transition, the uniformity of the edits becomes detectable. Apply rules unevenly: some paragraphs get heavy editing, others barely change. The distribution of interventions should itself be irregular. (Note: em-dashes are never a valid human intervention; see absolute_rules AR-002.) This is a Tier-2 principle: it applies to stylistic moves (word choice, transitions, closers, contrasts, texture). It does not apply to Tier-1 prohibitions (em-dashes and banned structures), which must always be eliminated. See foundation.enforcement.non_uniformity_scope.

core_caveats.statement: Newer, larger models are converging on human-like lexical distributions while retaining detectability through structural and psycholinguistic uniformity.
core_caveats.explanation: Lexical rules (flagged words, vocabulary diversity) become less reliable as newer models match human word distributions. Structural rules (repeated sentence shapes, sentence variation), discourse rules (transition patterns) and psycholinguistic texture (cognitive load artifacts, self-monitoring traces) become relatively more important. When prioritizing edits, weight the structural and psycholinguistic layers higher than lexical substitution for text that may have been generated by frontier models.
core_caveats.history: O'Sullivan (2025) shows GPT-4 clusters more tightly than GPT-3.5 in stylometric analysis. Przystalski et al. (2024) confirm that more complex models are harder to differentiate from human text at the lexical level. Kobak et al. (Science Advances 2025) and Kuznetsov et al. (arXiv:2501.19301, 2025) extend this through 2024-2025.

core_caveats.statement: The durable human/AI distinction lives in local flow and section-to-section variation, not in word-order-independent surface statistics.
core_caveats.explanation: Current models already match human text on word-order-independent features such as part-of-speech and stopword distributions and readability scores. The features that still diverge capture the flow of the text: how predictable each word is in its place, how the content changes through the piece, and how the style shifts between sections (structural_patterns.cross_segment_variation). Surface word substitution is necessary hygiene with a low ceiling. For text that may be from a frontier model, weight the structural and discourse layers higher.
core_caveats.history: Kuznetsov et al. (arXiv:2501.19301, 2025): humans modulate their fingerprint between a document's intro, body, and conclusion while LLMs hold one flat fingerprint throughout. Paraphrasing evades most detectors (Krishna et al., NeurIPS 2023), yet AI 'generation patterns' survive paraphrasing even as semantics drift (arXiv:2511.00416, 2025), and only detector-guided adversarial paraphrase reliably evades (arXiv:2506.07001, NeurIPS 2025), by destroying those flow features.

core_caveats.statement: Average sentence length does not distinguish AI from human text; only the variance does.
core_caveats.explanation: Studies disagree on the direction of mean sentence length, and it fails as a discriminator under scrutiny. The reliable structural signal is low VARIANCE in sentence length, not a particular average. humanizer_check_text reports the spread as metrics.length_stdev (see foundation.two_axes.burstiness). It is a number that describes the draft, never a finding or a target. Do not push sentences toward an average length or a spread; recombine or split them by meaning and let the number follow.

core_caveats.statement: A self-aware flourish (a neat closer, a meta label, a paradox headline) is a low-ceiling tell. The device is legitimate in moderation, so flag it as a judgment call.
core_caveats.explanation: Generated prose reaches for a satisfying beat (a closer, a frame, a reveal) because it optimizes for surface polish over saying one more true, specific thing, and these beats are topic-agnostic (the same closer could end almost any essay). But a single strong aphorism or a genuine paradox title can be entirely human. The rule targets repetition and a beat that stands in for content, so it is surfaced as a self_review judgment item and stays out of the hard prohibitions. This fits flow_over_surface_features, where content and flow beat surface flourish. The one mechanizable slice, a standalone meta label that names the artifact's own format or length ('in 200 words', 'in brief', 'at a high level') in place of its subject, is detected deterministically as BS-022 (checklist, never hard), scoped to bounded standalone labels so embedded uses are not flagged.

core_caveats.statement: Em-dash frequency is a model-specific signal, not a universal statistical AI tell, but the AR-002 ban still stands.
core_caveats.explanation: Em-dash production varies widely by model, from almost none in some open models to several per 1,000 words in others, so the em-dash is not a reliable detector on its own. This does NOT relax absolute_rules AR-002. The ban rests on how the writing reads to a human reader, which the detector data does not change. Keep eliminating em-dashes regardless. Do not treat the absence of em-dashes as evidence a text is human, and do not over-index on em-dashes alone.
core_caveats.history: Measured range: roughly 0.0 per 1,000 words (Llama 3.1/3.3) up to about 9-10 per 1,000 words (GPT-4.1); reporting concludes the 'ChatGPT hyphen' is not a reliable detector on its own (Washington Post 2025; Indiana Capital Chronicle 2025); the mechanism is plausibly markdown training leaking into prose. The ban was justified by reading and by this project's own history, not by statistical detectability.

core_caveats.statement: The prose metrics are meaningless on headline, label and fragment text, and the structural coverage is prose-shaped, so short copy can fail the checker spuriously and pass it undeservedly. On such copy, read the prohibitions and set the metrics aside.
core_caveats.explanation: Labels have no sentences to vary, so the length numbers and segment_uniformity measure a property the text does not have, and acting on them would mean padding headings into sentences. The banned_structures are frames drawn from prose, so an empty evaluative subtitle such as 'Eight words to carry' or 'Your answer first' can pass. Run the check on label copy and on deliberately simple body text (teaching material pitched at a CEFR level, UI strings, captions). Read hard_violations, the banned_structures and the lexical flags, which stay meaningful at any length. Ignore the length numbers and segment_uniformity; on CEFR-pitched prose the flat short sentences are what the specification asks for. Skipping the run would leave the em-dash ban and the phrase-frame structures unchecked on student-facing copy. The server does not guess that an input is labels, because a guess from length or punctuation would misfire on ordinary short-form prose. The caller can declare short copy with content_type 'label' or 'notes' on humanizer_check_text, which still reports the length numbers and segment_variation under metrics (length_metrics_apply false) but does not list segment_uniformity as a must_clear finding.
core_caveats.history: Measured on the chrome of a slide deck (11 act names, slide titles and section descriptors, checked as one document): the report came back prohibitions_clear with a sentence-length stdev of 1.0 on a mean sentence length of 3.5 words, and missed two AI-register tells in its input. A 139-word B1 slide set returned prohibitions_clear with zero hard violations. Documented rather than detected on purpose: a checker that cries wolf gets ignored. The content_type declaration is explicit, so it differs from the rejected length-guessing heuristic.

core_caveats.statement: Headings, subtitles and deks carry AI tells that the prose rules were never shaped to catch, and the tells there lie in the frame of the label more than in its words. Check the labels of a piece as their own pass, and read the repeated shape rather than any single line.
core_caveats.explanation: A label can name its subject and then annex a second element promising the subject matters, as a WH clause ('Method, and why this one') or as a reduced relative ('Reintegration support at the moment of release from Canadian federal prison, and the officer the whole system turns on.'). Only the WH form is mechanized, as BS-038. Telling the reduced-relative form apart from ordinary coordination ('Bread, and the flour that makes it') needs to know whether the head is a verbless noun phrase, which needs a parser, so the appositive family is a self_review judgment item with a budget of one per document. Read this together with caveats.metrics_do_not_apply_to_label_text: on label input the metrics are undefined, and the structural coverage is thin. The section symbol and middot separators are typography conventions and say nothing about authorship.

core_caveats.statement: Orwell's rule 5 has a carve-out this server enforces: a domain term with no everyday equivalent is defined in plain words at first use and then used plainly. It is never swapped for a vaguer ordinary word.
core_caveats.explanation: The rule as written ('never use a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent') is conditional, and the condition fails more often than the rule's popularity suggests. A term of art frequently names something no ordinary word names: 'statutory release' is not 'automatic release', 'Protected B' is not 'confidential', a subpoena is not a request. Substituting the everyday word does not simplify the sentence, it changes what the sentence claims, which puts the rule in direct conflict with AR-001. The failure Orwell was attacking is jargon reached for to avoid a plain statement, not jargon used because it is correct. So the test is whether an everyday word means the same thing, and where it does not, the fix is a definition at first use and then the term. Reads together with lexical_patterns.orwell.jargon_carve_out, which carries the worked example.
core_caveats.history: Recorded 2026-08-10 from a case-study gate where the Orwell layer had to be carved out by hand for eight corrections-domain terms, because a naive pass over them would have deleted the precision the whole argument ran on.

core_caveats.statement: Several rules budget a shape at one instance per piece. humanizer_check_text counts only within the text it is handed, so a section-by-section walk can clear every run while the assembled document holds four. The last run must be on the whole document.
core_caveats.explanation: The one-per-piece budgets (BS-011 and BS-039 for the antithesis, BS-038 and the appended-label rubric item, the aphorism in the performative-framing item, BS-018's copula maxim) rest on repetition being the signal. One instance is ordinary writing; the same shape three times reads as machine-made. The checker is stateless and per-call, and a long document is usually written and checked section by section, so each call sees one instance and reports a single finding a writer can reasonably justify. banned_structures entries carry a document_budget (BS-011, BS-018, BS-038 and BS-039, each budget 1), and humanizer_check_text reports a document_budget finding when a budgeted shape appears more often than its budget in one call. It still sees only the text it is handed, so the last run must be on the assembled document (foundation.application_protocol phase 9). The budgeted items that need judgment (the appositive significance label, the aphorism, the anaphoric run) stay in the self_review rubric, because a detector that cannot find one instance cannot count three.
core_caveats.history: Found 2026-08-10 on a 39-page case study where the appended-significance label had been justified four separate times, once per section, and the pattern was only visible when the sections were read together. The mechanical fix, a document-level count of budgeted structures, was scoped out rather than rejected. UPDATE 2026-09-18: the mechanical half now exists for the shapes a detector can find. loader.load_document_budgets reads the document_budget field and src/checker/budgets.py emits the finding; the finding says in its own text that the last run must be on the assembled document.

core_caveats.statement: Short worksheet-cell prose can pass the checker clean while a reader still hears it as machine-written, because the tells in it are semantic figures that no fixed phrase captures. Four of them are mechanized, three at low confidence and BS-053 at medium.
core_caveats.explanation: The tells in worksheet cells fall into three families: a time noun as the agent of a survival or predation verb ('Co-op hours were 9 to 5, so the Fridays survived.', 'Busy season eats the Fridays.', 'Billiards survives final year.', 'Work does not get to claim them.'), the clipped retention verdict ('The Scouts books and the tutoring stay.', 'Tutoring stays.') and the deictic stance closer ('Seven to eight hours of sleep, and I want to keep it there.'). The 'get my Fridays back' / 'have my evenings back' refrain is a fourth. BS-052, BS-054 and BS-055 (budget-only) cover them at confidence 'low' and BS-053 at 'medium'. The attested examples also sit in the self_review rubric. 'Fine. The dog stays.' is an accepted residual. The aphoristic closers in the same cells ('four months is a long time to wait', 'tires me out more than any lecture did') are not mechanized and are a rubric example under the performative framing beat.

core_caveats.statement: Most default-style prose from current Claude models passes this checker with two findings or fewer, so a clean report is weak evidence that a draft reads as human.
core_caveats.explanation: The tells a reader still notices in default-style prose sit mostly in the closers (a tidy maxim, an upbeat forecast, an importance flag), which BS-062 to BS-064 cover in part. Published tells are model-specific and age fast, so a rule needs a sample from the models people are using now as well as a paper. Run the self-review rubric even when must_clear is empty.
core_caveats.history: Measured 2026-10-30. For the research round of 2026-10-30, 32 pieces of default-style prose were generated by Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku across 16 genres, with no style guidance, and run through humanizer_check_text before any new rule existed. 21 of the 32 came back with two findings or fewer, and none had a hard violation. The tells a reader would still notice were mostly in the closers (a tidy maxim, an upbeat forecast, an importance flag), which BS-062..BS-064 now cover in part. Two findings with strong published effect sizes did NOT transfer: present participial clause density (5.3 times the human rate in GPT-4o, Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025) flagged 4.1 percent of sentences in the Claude sample against 5.6 percent in pre-2022 Wikipedia, and coordinated nominalization pairs ('transparency and accountability') appeared 0 times in the sample against 12 to 37 per 10k sentences of human prose. Published tells are model-specific and age fast, so a rule needs a sample from the models people are using now, not only a paper. Run the self-review rubric even when must_clear is empty.

core_caveats.statement: Every line a human editor flagged as AI-coded in a month of portfolio copy had passed this checker, so on that kind of copy the self_review rubric carries the detection.
core_caveats.explanation: The shapes the editor flagged differ from legitimate lines only in meaning, so no regex separates them. The numeral-contrast caption ('One count, four moments') reads like dosing, box scores, listings and headlines ('Two tablets, every four hours.', 'Two adults, one child.'). These shapes are carried as self_review items: the cause-to-benefit 'so' tail, backstory order and self-portrait flourish, the cold-reader test, and additions to abstraction-as-agent and performative framing (which holds the numeric caption). A clean report on product, portfolio or case-study copy says little until those items have been read.
core_caveats.history: Measured 2026-11-09. Between 2026-10-11 and 2026-11-05 the owner of a portfolio site reviewed copy written by Claude and flagged 31 lines as AI-coded, empty or unclear for a first-time reader. Run through humanizer_check_text on 2026-11-09, all 31 returned prohibitions_clear with no structural finding. Five shapes were probed as regex rules against Tier 1, Tier 2, pre-2022 essays and pre-2022 Wikipedia; none survived. The closest, the numeral-contrast caption ('One count, four moments'), measured zero on all four corpora but an adversarial review found about 100 legitimate lines it flags, such as dosing, box scores, listings and headlines ('Two tablets, every four hours.', 'Two adults, one child.'), which differ from the tell only in meaning. Everything is carried as self_review items: the cause-to-benefit 'so' tail, backstory order and self-portrait flourish, the cold-reader test, and additions to abstraction-as-agent and performative framing (which now holds the numeric caption). A clean report on product, portfolio or case-study copy therefore says little until those items have been read honestly.

ethical_considerations.statement: This system is designed to improve the quality and readability of AI-assisted writing, not to disguise AI authorship where disclosure is required.
guidance: Where institutional or legal requirements mandate disclosure of AI involvement in content creation, this system should be used alongside (not instead of) appropriate disclosure.
The goal is better writing, not deception. Human-patterned text is more readable, more engaging, and more effective regardless of its authorship.
When human oversight is applied during editing, the resulting text is human-edited, which is a legitimate description of the process.

maintainer_notes.statement: When a deliberate rhetorical figure and its abusive twin are the same construction, no shape detector can separate them — the difference is whether the repetition earns itself, which is not a property of the string.
maintainer_notes.explanation: Measured on anaphora (three or more consecutive sentences opening on the same word), 2026-09-18. Every formulation was probed against 47,088 sentences of pre-1930 public-domain prose (Bleak House, Pride and Prejudice, Moby-Dick, Walden, Tom Sawyer, Sherlock Holmes). The loosest scored 75.4 false positives per 10k sentences; the best (same first two tokens, threshold three, every sentence at most ten words) scored 3.2 per 10k with 6/6 recall, and all fifteen of its firings were read and found legitimate — 0/15 precision. They include Thoreau's 'It does not keep the country free. It does not settle the West. It does not educate.' and Melville's 'Forty years of continual whaling!' Set against the attested model tell 'It reflects the brief. It reflects the budget. It reflects the deadline.', every readable property is identical: three sentences, subject pronoun plus repeated verb, under eight words each, paragraph-internal. Unlike labels_are_where_the_tells_hide, a parser would not help, because the two cases are the same construction rather than different ones that look alike. Raising the threshold to four scored 0/6 recall while still firing, so it is strictly dominated. The already-deployed BS-009 (this_chain) returns 27 findings on the same corpus, 5.7 per 10k, twelve of them in Walden — it is kept because it is gate=checklist and narrow, but it is not clean, and a later round should start from that number rather than assume it. The tell is carried by the self_review rubric instead. Do not re-attempt without a corpus of attested in-the-wild model anaphora, which is the missing input, not a new formulation. Confirmed a second time on 2026-09-18, on a different rule: rule_of_three_density returns 97 findings on the same corpus, 20.6 per 10k, 31 in Bleak House and 36 in Moby-Dick, and all of them are catalogues or triadic description (the shop-inscription list, 'short, cadaverous, and withered', the stationer's inventory). That is what this caveat predicted before the sweep ran, so the detector was read and deliberately left unchanged: it is gate=checklist, it lives in src/checker/structures.py so a change would cost a rebuild, and the only readable knobs (item count, clustering window) were already probed when it shipped in June.

maintainer_notes.statement: eval/corpus/human averages under seven sentences per file, so it cannot falsify any rule that needs a run of consecutive sentences. A 0/16 pass from it is not evidence for such a rule. Each eval tier has a blind spot, and a round must say which tier answers its question.
maintainer_notes.explanation: The calibration corpus is 16 files and 109 sentences in total. Any cross-sentence or run-length detector (an anaphora chain, a uniformity measure, a three-in-a-row structure) has almost no room to fire in a seven-sentence document, so it scores 0/16 whatever its real precision. Demonstrated 2026-09-18: eight anaphora formulations all scored 0/16, including one that measures 75.4 false positives per 10k sentences on long-form human prose. The zeros held (a control positive fired on all eight), which is what makes the trap quiet: the harness is working and the number says nothing. The same limitation applies to segment_uniformity, which needs three or more sections. Resolved the same week by splitting the bar in two. A run-length or document-scoped rule is now measured on a second tier of six pre-1930 works, 47,088 sentences, and reported as a rate per 10k sentences rather than a raw count, with every firing read. That tier has the mirror-image blind spot: 22 of the 40 deployed regex structures score exactly zero on it, because Victorian fiction contains no marketing copy, meta-labels or corporate abstraction. So a zero on either tier is only reportable when a discriminating control fired in the same pipeline on the same run, since a sweep that found nothing and a sweep that cannot fire produce identical output.

maintainer_notes.statement: A scope note and the contrastive tell are one construction. 'The tell is the appending, not the phrase.' and 'The work is judgement, not process.' differ in what the writer is doing, not in anything a pattern can read, so BS-011 accepts the scope-note firing rather than pretending to separate it.
maintainer_notes.explanation: Measured 2026-09-18 while replacing BS-011. The deployed two-token pattern fired 358 times on 47,088 sentences of pre-1930 prose, 76.0 per 10k, the worst rate of any rule in the server, on ordinary negation such as 'not yet decided' and 'not more than nineteen'; it declined 1 of 6 constructed hard negatives. The copula-anchored replacement scores 0 firings there with 6/6 recall on the attested tells and 6/6 on the hard negatives. That zero sits in Tier 2's blind spot: Victorian fiction never writes a sentence whose job is to fix the scope of a rule it just stated. On a modern control of 30 markdown files already on disk (this repo's docs and specs plus the sibling humanize-text-prompt), 2,692 sentences, the same pattern fires 9 times, 33.4 per 10k. All nine were read: eight are scope notes and one is the round's own attested tell quoted as evidence, so precision is 1/9. Narrowing further was probed and fails, because determiners, sentence position and a prestige-noun lexicon all cut across the two senses rather than between them. The rule ships anyway because it beats the incumbent on every measured axis at gate=checklist, where a false positive costs one justification. The corresponding recall loss is real and deliberate: contrastives outside the copula frame, including AP-005's own before-text, are no longer detected and are carried by the self_review rubric. The modern control was deliberately NOT promoted to a third corpus tier: 8 of its 9 firings are in prose about this very construction, so it is a biased sample, and an unbiased modern corpus is still in copyright. The eight accepted false positives are pinned as tests in tests/checker/test_bs011_copula_anchor.py instead.

maintainer_notes.statement: A false-positive rate measured per layer is meaningless for the flagged-term lexicon. The 5.0 per 10k threshold was calibrated for one detector and one reader; 120 lexicon groups sharing a finding type must be compared per term.
maintainer_notes.explanation: Measured 2026-09-18. flagged_term returns 164 findings on 47,088 sentences of pre-1930 prose, 34.8 per 10k, from 655 word occurrences, the largest contributors being particularly (117), Moreover (45), Consequently (39), endeavor (39), boast (35), elevate (35), landscape (32) and commence (31). Every one is the pre-tell sense of ordinary formal vocabulary, which is over_regularization_caveat working as described. The rate is the wrong instrument: the 5.0 threshold was set by what one person can audit for a single rule (about 24 firings), and this layer is roughly 120 groups, so per group the rate is 0.29 per 10k. The same lexicon also fires 10 times on the calibration corpus (109 sentences of modern human prose) on Additionally, foster, innovative, facilitate, harness, cornerstone, boast, particularly, refine and differentiate, each once or twice, so the behaviour is register-independent and known rather than a Victorian artifact. Collocation scoping of the kind BS-033 applied to 'quiet' was considered and does not transfer: that word's tell IS a collocation, whereas delve, bolster and enhance are flagged for clustering and frequency, which content_profiles and the severity field already adjust for. Kept unchanged at gate=checklist, where a firing costs one justification. A future round comparing a lexicon against a corpus must report per term.

The 2026-08-08 report that produced BS-038 was of a document that had passed the 2026-08-06 checker clean: every finding the reviewer could name sat in the chrome. Two of them were the same move, a label that names its subject and then annexes a second element promising the subject matters, once as a WH clause ('Method, and why this one') and once as a reduced relative ('Reintegration support at the moment of release from Canadian federal prison, and the officer the whole system turns on.'). Only the WH form is mechanized. Separating the reduced-relative form from ordinary coordination ('Bread, and the flour that makes it') needs to know whether the head is a verbless noun phrase, which needs a parser this server does not have and will not get: the lexical approximations tried during the build all misfired on one-sentence paragraphs, which under a no-hard-wrap markdown convention are indistinguishable from label lines. So the appositive family is a self_review judgment item, and this caveat records why the gap is deliberate. Reads together with metrics_do_not_apply_to_label_text, which covers the other half of the same blind spot: on label input the metrics are undefined, and here the structural coverage is thin. Two candidate signals from the same report were rejected as not authorship evidence at all: the section symbol, which is ordinary in anything citing statute, and middot separators, which are a typography convention as common in human-authored web copy as in generated copy. Flagging either would repeat the smart-quote mistake of 2026-07-13, where a tooling artifact was mistaken for an author signal. Re-tested on 2026-09-17 after the same shape was reported again, and the rejection holds with numbers this time. A loose pattern carrying BS-038's guards scored 3/3 recall and 10/10 false positives on ordinary coordination with a non-pronoun subject ('The baker bought bread, and the flour that makes it.'); the zero on the human corpus is absence of the shape, not discrimination. A density gate firing only at two or more per document was rejected on reasoning: a density gate works when the individual instances are legitimate and the clustering is the signal, which is why rule_of_three_density and segment_uniformity work, whereas here per-instance precision is zero and a threshold of two only means two ordinary sentences trip it. A finite-verb blocklist on the head scored 4/5 recall and 1/14 false positives, against a standing bar of zero on constructed literal probes: the miss was 'The revised release policy, and the parole officer at its centre', where the -ed guard eats the past-participle modifiers common in this very register, and the false positive was 'The vendor ships on Tuesday, and the invoice follows', where the third-person-singular list is open by nature. Precision and recall trade against each other through a part-of-speech boundary a regex cannot see. The shape stays a self_review judgment item with a stated budget of one per document.

Recorded 2026-09-29 from a real drafting session: a B2 student exemplar written in worksheet cells returned prohibitions_clear with no lexical or structural findings, and a human reviewer flagged six phrases. They fell into three families: a time noun as the agent of a survival or predation verb ('Co-op hours were 9 to 5, so the Fridays survived.', 'Busy season eats the Fridays.', 'Billiards survives final year.', 'Work does not get to claim them.'), the clipped retention verdict ('The Scouts books and the tutoring stay.', 'Tutoring stays.') and the deictic stance closer ('Seven to eight hours of sleep, and I want to keep it there.'). A second pass added the 'get my Fridays back' / 'have my evenings back' refrain. These are BS-052, BS-053, BS-054 and BS-055 (budget-only). Recall is 9/9, 7/7, 3/3 and 2/2 on the attested and constructed positives, with 0 false positives on 62 adversarial negatives. An independent review of the first draft predicted 26 failures by hand ('I barely survived the semester', 'Questions remain.', 'No one stays.', 'I want to keep it up') and all 26 reproduced, which is why BS-052 now needs a determiner, object pronoun or sentence end after the verb, BS-053 dropped 'remains', and BS-054 needs a number to point back at. 'Fine. The dog stays.' is an accepted residual. Only BS-053 has a real corpus measurement: a loose version of it fires 18 times on the 47,088-sentence Tier 2 corpus and the shipped rule fires 0 times, although reading those 18 is how its first guards were chosen, so that zero is partly fitted. For the other three, loose controls fire 0, 1 and 2 times across Tier 1, Tier 2 and the modern control together, because Victorian novels and repository docs almost never use weekday or semester nouns as subjects. Their zero is blind, so they ship at confidence 'low' and the attested examples also sit in the self_review rubric. What would fix this is a modern, casual-register human corpus (personal essays, student writing) where these frames actually occur. The aphoristic closers the same review flagged ('four months is a long time to wait', 'tires me out more than any lecture did') are not mechanized and are a rubric example under the performative framing beat.
